86 (1987) 27-38 27 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V., Amsterdam - Printed in The Netherlands [51 A paleomagnetic reinvestigation of the Upper Devonian Perry Formation: evidence for Late Paleozoic remagnetization Carola Stearns and Rob Van der Voo Department of Geological Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1063 (U.S.A) Received June 3, 1987; revised version received August 22, 1987 In view of the recent recognition of widespread Late Paleozoic remagnetization of Devonian formations across North America, we undertook a reinvestigation of the Upper Devonian Perry Formation of coastal Maine and adjacent New Brunswick. Thermal demagnetization of samples from the redbeds yielded a characteristic direction (D = 166 ° l = 4 °) that fails a fold test. Introduction Recent recognition of widespread Permocar- boniferous remagnetization of several Devonian formations across North America [1-6] has led to a re-evaluation of the existing Devonian paleo- magnetic data presented in earlier studies. Because many of the earlier studies did not recognize or completely remove secondary components of mag- netization, the results of these studies have had to be revised. One of the results of this re-evaluation has been a decrease in the number of reliable Devonian paleomagnetic poles for North America. In fact, in a recent review of North American Paleozoic paleomagnetism, Van der Voo [7] lists only two reliable Devonian poles for the craton of North America. It has been shown that many of the existing cratonic reference poles are in fact based on Kiaman remagnetizations [7,8]. Clearly it has become increasingly important to reinvestigate the published Devonian results from the 1960s in order to determine the reliability of the poles. Modern laboratory and data-analytical techniques have improved our ability to isolate components of magnetization and to identify rocks that carry secondary magnetizations. They reported unstable behavior for the basalts, ran- dom directions from a rhyolite, and two poorly resolved components of magnetization from the redbeds. Introduction The magnetic polarity time scale for the Late Cretaceous and Cenozoic has been established by the correlation of marine magnetic anomalies with magnetostratigraphic sequences in sedimentary and volcanic rocks [1]. The correlation of the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous M-sequence anoma- lies with magnetostratigraphic studies in pelagic limestones sequences has been only partially established [2-4]. However, there is no oceanic crust known to be older than Middle Jurassic. Thus, the Early Jurassic magnetic polarity time scale cannot be derived from marine magnetic anomalies and must be established from magnetostratigraphic studies. Among sedimentary rock sequences, stratotype sections are the best documented ones with multi- ple biostratigraphic bed to bed analysis and, par- ticularly during Jurassic times, with detailed am- monite zonation. The Toarcian stratotype was one of the chosen sections for two main reasons: (1) previous magnetostratigraphic studies which have investigated sedimentary rocks of Lower Jurassic age are scarce [5-7], (2) good correlation tools are needed for drillings projects, especially through the Toarcian series,

Lower Jurassic age are scarce [5-7], (2) good correlation tools are needed for drillings projects, especially through the Toarcian series, well known as oil-source sedi- mentary facies in the French Paris Basin. 0012-821X/88/$03.50 © 1988 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. No radiometric data can be strictly attributed to the Toarcian stage, but it seems that this rela- tively long stage (8 ammonites zones) extends from 181 to 189 Ma [8]. We have sampled two sections in the southwest part of the Paris Basin: the Toarcian stratotype near Thouars and a complementary section in Airvault (20 km southeast) in order to build a magnetic polarity pattern. The results have yielded a magnetic polarity zonation and have provided very good biostratigraphic ages of the reversals based on an ammonite horizon scale. They have also located lacunae in the sedimentary record, better than with the ammonite zonation tool. 2. Introduction To a first approximation, the time-averaged earth's magnetic field is an axial geocentric dipole [ 1,2]. Although this seems to hold true for most of the observed data, there have often been anomalous results which require alternative explanations. The most obvious inconsistency is the tendency for inclinations from Cenozoic units to be different from those predicted for the site latitude using the axial geocentric dipole. More recently Cox [10] has suggested that westward movement of the drifting part of the nondipole field could account for these inclination anomalies observed in Recent and Quaternary data. More recently Cox [10] has suggested that westward movement of the drifting part of the nondipole field could account for these inclination anomalies observed in Recent and Quaternary data. The VGPs determined from this study on 21 lava flows from the Medicine Lake High- lands show a larger than usual offset, and have corre- sponding inclinations too shallow for the axial dipole model by 12 ° . 2. samples come from an area which lies north of a major ophiolite zone that recent workers suggest is the southwestern continuation of the Indus Suture. As the present palaeomagnetic results are in fair agreement with palaeomagnetic data from the Siberian platform but not with data from Gondwanaland they can be taken as additional evidence that this suture does indeed constitute the main collision zone between the Gondwanic Indian subcontinent and Asia. The palaeomagnetic data presented here from the Devonian of Chitral suggests additionally: (1) in excess of 100 ° of counterclockwise rotation of the area, associated most likely with the formation of the regional Hindukush-Pamir-Karakoram syntaxial bend; (2) more than 2000 km of crustal shortening between Chitral and the Siberian platform due to the northward indentation of the Indian Gondwanaland fragment subsequent to collision. 1. The Devonian succession in the thrust sheet at Kur~gh consists largely of competent rocks, predominantly carbonates and quartzites which, though steeply tilted and locally dislocated by minor faults and folds, are not otherwise penetratively deformed or detectably metamorphosed. The un- metamorphosed nature of the section is witnessed by the absence of greenschist grade metamorphic miner- als and by the excellent preservation of shelly fossils (with unrecrystallized skeletal fabrics) and plant fossils at different stratigraphic levels (Fig. 2). The samples were collected from three sedimentary chamositic ironstone units that occur at separate levels within an interval of approximately 100 m beginning about 60 m above the base of the Upper Devonian part of the succession (Fig. 2). This is to be regretted as the Indian plate under- went a fast northward movement of large magnitude during the latest Mesozoic and the earliest Cenozoic. Detailed knowledge about the palaeolatitudinal posi- tion of the Indian plate during this period is essential for evaluation of the various collision models. The movement of the Indian plate relative to Australia is rathei well detailed nowadays from marine magnetic anomaly studies [55,75-78], but for geographical positioning of the Indian plate such studies relied on the Australian apparent polar wander (APW) curve [79]. The paleomagnetic pole position was calculated from the mean ChRM direction following structural correction (Table 1). Introduction Several attempts have been made to correlate magnetozones recorded in Jurassic-Cretaceous sedimentary sections with the M-sequence of marine magnetic anomalies. These magnetostrati- graphic investigations were carried out on the Maiolica pelagic limestones in Italy [1-4], the Am- monitico Rosso limestone in the Southern Alps [5], the Sumeg section in Hungary [6] and deep-sea sediments (DSDP, Site 534) [7]. Geolog~ The Cordillera de la Costa, Antofagasta Prov- ince, comprises rocks ranging in age from Pre- cambrian [18] to Quaternary [19] and is bounded to the east by the Atacama fault zone (Fig. la). Exposure is generally good, and it is dominated by the apparently 10 km thick, volcanic La Negra Formation [20], and associated acid to inter- mediate Jurassic and limited Cretaceous plutons [19]. Further south in the Chanaral district exten- sive Jurassic gabbros occur within the Cordillera de la Costa [21]. In Antofagasta Province, the plutons range in age from 159 to 134 Ma [19,22] and intrude the mid-Jurassic La Negra Formation [22]. The La Negra Formation and plutons have been interpreted as representing the relicts of a volcanic island arc [23--25]. Rijswijk (The Netherlands') Received January 28, 1988: revised version accepted June 3, 1988 Palaeomagnetic studies of Lower Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous volcanic, plutonic and sedimentary rocks from the Cordillera de la Costa of northern Chile, indicate that there has been no significant latitudinal movement of northern Chile since early Cretaceous times. A palaeomagnetic pole for the Cordillera de la Costa (63°S, 187 ° E: a,~ s = 7.7 ° ) was derived from combining the results of three studied units, the La Negra Formation (Jurassic volcanics): Jurassic/Lower Cretaceous granodioritic plutons; and the El Way Formation (Hauterivian marine carbonates) together with the Coloso Formation (Lower Cretaceous red beds). Comparison with a Cretaceous reference pole for the stable shield area of South America (87 o S, 235 o E; a,as = 2.4 o ) indicates that 24 + 7 o of clockwise rotation has taken place. Possible mechanisms for the rotation of the Andean forearc in this area have been examined in relation to the kinetics of the subducting Nazca and over-riding South American plates. The Cordillera de la Costa has been subjected to both compressional and extensional

kinetics of the subducting Nazca and over-riding South American plates. The Cordillera de la Costa has been subjected to both compressional and extensional tectonics since the I,ower Cretaceous. Major eastwardly directed thrusting in mid-Cretaceous and early Tertiary times, possibly associated with a period of oblique subduction of the Nazca plate, contributed to the accretion of the Cordillera to the main forearc; rotation may have occurred during this process. Introduction Several independent analyses of palaeomagnet- ic data have identified large apparent polar wander (APW) movements during Late Precambrian and Lower Cambrian times which imply high rates of continental movement during this interval. This is specifically seen in APW segments which contrast with the Upper Palaeozoic and younger paths (e.g. [1]) and the long latitudinal movement of the Gondwanaland path [2] which corresponds with the incidence of late Precambrian and Cambrian glaciation [3]. The scale of APW during these times is currently best defined from studies within the former supercontinent of Gondwanaland [3]; the definition and dating of these movements is, however, hampered by the paucity of igneous material of this a

(Fig. 5). Unfortunately Vendian to Cambrian data from this crustal block are not yet adequate to properly define the preceding and succeeding paths connecting with this segment. The Fen results appear to continue a movement defined by results from dyke swarms (results 1, 2 and 3 in Table 2 and Fig. 5) recording episodes of late Precambrian fracturing within the Fennoscandian Shield. The path may then extend to a result from a steep component in the ca. 40 Ma younger Alni5 Com- plex (pole 7); however, this latter pole is computed from a steep positive remanence which may be dominated by younger overprints. The predomi- nant dual polarity axis in the Alni5 body (pole 8) has a shallow inclination and a return of this block to low palaeolatitudes during Lower Cambrian times is also suggested by a result from the Nexo Sandstone (pole 6). Many more studies will be required to evaluate the detail of this APW path and they will, unfortunately, have to focus on sedimentary material. The Slockenray Formation is Arenig in age [8,9] which accords well with radiometric de- terminations elsewhere in the ophiolite sum- marised by Hamilton et al. [10]. Macrofossil evi- dence from a lateral equivalent of the overlying Benan Conglomerate dates the unit as of Llandeilo age [11,12]. Previous palaeomagnetic results from the ophiolite (i.e. [13,14]) have been incorporated with other British Ordovician data in apparent polar wander schemes (e.g. [15,16]). This carries the assumption of a post-obduction origin for the recovered magnetisations as no accretion related deformation was accounted for. The present study was therefore aimed at the uncovering of "primary" or pre-obduction mag- netisations using more detailed demagnetisation analyses compared with these earlier studies. Also the availability of a detailed map of this part of the complex affords the opportunity to deal with structural complexity using the palaeomagnetic data interactively. It was hoped that constraints might then be placed with respect to the tectonic evolution of the ophiolite in the context of the British Caledonides. 2. uses on the Slockenray Formation of the northern belt. This unit is comprised of a sequence of spilitic lavas together with a variety of intercalated sedi- ments. The present investigation considers sam- ples from all the exposed lithologies of the Sloc- kenray Formation including an intra-formational conglomeratic facies. An additional palaeomagnetic conglomerate test was performed in the Benan Conglomerate of mixed source provenance containing volcanic clasts likely derived from the Ballantrae Ophiolite. Late Paleozoic faunas indicate that by this time the Oaxaca Terrane was once again associated with North America. In an attempt to gain further insight into the drift history of this area, we have undertaken a paleomagnetic study of the Paleozoic sedimentary rocks of Oaxaca. The results of our study indicate that the entire Paleozoic section was remagnetized in the same paleomagnetic field at some time following late Paleozoic sedimentation, emplacement of an igneous complex, and the earlier of two folding events. Fold and conglomerate tests show that the remagnetization occurred prior to deposition and folding of overlying early Cretaceous sediments. The Oaxaca Paleozoic rocks were therefore remagnetized sometime between late Permian and early Cretaceous. Since the exact age of remagnetization is not known, we compare our result with data from cratonic North America for the bracketed range of magnetization ages. This analysis indicates that as much as 28 o of net counterclockwise rotation could have occurred between Oaxaca and cratonic North America subsequent to the Oaxaca remagnetization. 1. Palaeomagnetism of Palaeozoic inliers, northern England The major Lower Palaeozoic igneous episode in the north of England is represented by the Borrow- dale Volcanic Series which occupies the larger part of the Lake District inlier (Fig. l). It comprises a pile of intermediate to acid lavas and tufts erupted between the late Llanvirn and Lower Caradoc stages of Ordovi- cian time [8] and locally reaches a thickness of 7000 m. Pataeomagnetic results were reported by Morris [9] and Faller et al. [10] and these are combined in Table 2 with four additional sites reported by Piper et al. [11] ; with the exception of three sites [9], this work was concentrated on the lower part of the vol- canic succession. Additional work will be necessary to evaluate the magnetic stratigraphy and the significance of the high percentage of anomalous directions found by the earlier workers. Tire upper part of the Borrowdale Volcanic Series has accordingly been sampled where detailed struc- tural and stratigraphic control is available (based on the field studies of Mitchell [12]). Palaeomagnetism of Palaeozoic inliers, northern England The major Lower Palaeozoic igneous episode in the north of England is represented by the Borrow- dale Volcanic Series which occupies the larger part of the Lake District inlier (Fig. l). It comprises a pile of intermediate to acid lavas and tufts erupted between the late Llanvirn and Lower Caradoc stages of Ordovi- cian time [8] and locally reaches a thickness of 7000 m. Pataeomagnetic results were reported by Morris [9] and Faller et al. [10] and these are combined in Table 2 with four additional sites reported by Piper et al. [11] ; with the exception of three sites [9], this work was concentrated on the lower part of the vol- canic succession. Additional work will be necessary to evaluate the magnetic stratigraphy and the significance of the high percentage of anomalous directions found by the earlier workers. Tire upper part of the Borrowdale Volcanic Series has accordingly been sampled where detailed struc- tural and stratigraphic control is available (based on the field studies of Mitchell [12]). All of these Proterozoic tectonic/magmatic trends are parallel to the long axis of the continental reconstruction. 1. Introduction Stabilisation and uplift of the widespread ca. 1800 m.y. (Churchill-Hudsonian, Ketilidian, Svecofennian- Svecokarelian) mobile belts within the Laurentian, Baltic and Ukrainian Shields, were followed by the intrusion of distinctive igneous rock suites in Middle- Upper Proterozoic times [1 ]. These include large plutons of massive anorthosites, rapakivi granites and alkaline complexes, basaltic and lamprophyric dyke swarms, and extensive suites of plateau basalts and ignimbrites; this was apparently the first time in Earth history that such associations began to form prominent rock groups [2]. Within these shields, they provide the main opportunity to sample the palaeo- magnetic field between the time of cooling of the ca. 1800 m.y. mobile belts and development of the late Proterozoic Sveconorwegian and Grenville mobile belts at ca. 1100-1000 m.y. Within these shields, they provide the main opportunity to sample the palaeo- magnetic field between the time of cooling of the ca. 1800 m.y. mobile belts and development of the late Proterozoic Sveconorwegian and Grenville mobile belts at ca. 1100-1000 m.y. This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of rapakivi-granite/massive anorthosite bodies within the Swedish part of the Baltic Shield. It also discusses the definition of the Proterozoic apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) path for this shield and examines the correla- tion between this path and the contemporaneous data from the Laurentian Shield. The geological implica- tions of these correlations are briefly examined. 444 2. Geological setting The bulk of the Swedish sector of the Baltic Shield consists of gneisses and granites affected by the Svecofennian (or Svecokarelian) mobile episode ending about 1800 m.y. [3]. The termination of tectonic activity is defined by the Rb-Sr isochron age of 1748 +__ 40 m.y.

In practice the hematite is an exsolution phase within accumulative feldspar, and the large magnetite grains shows clear evidence of being strongly resorbed: where associated with pyrrhotite they form rounded resorbed and anhedral grains with re-entrants. By contrast, the pyrrhotite grains are sometimes euhedral, form rami- fying veins, and are always interstitial; they may over- grow the magnetites and commonly form within re-entrants. Large magnetite grains are usually associated with magnetic remanence of low stability [23], and it is with this phase that the medium coercivity remanence of the gabbro-anorthosite probably resides. By con- trast fine needle-shaped grains of both magnetite [24] and hematite [25] are associated with high coer- civity remanence with high stability. The fine exsolved rods (apparently predominantly of hematite) within the feldspar megacrysts appear to be the most likely source of high coercivity remanence in the gabbro anorthosite facies of the complex. The geological implica- tions of these correlations are briefly examined. 444 2. Geological setting The bulk of the Swedish sector of the Baltic Shield consists of gneisses and granites affected by the Svecofennian (or Svecokarelian) mobile episode ending about 1800 m.y. [3]. The termination of tectonic activity is defined by the Rb-Sr isochron age of 1748 +__ 40 m.y.

However, based on the COCORP data the Brevard Zone is presently interpreted as a low-angle thrust fault related to the main horizontal fault that runs beneath the Appalachians [4]. Although much has been learned about the complex orogenic evolution of the Piedmont in recent years [5], it still remains one of the puzzling areas with poorly known geological rela- tionships. Intense deformation and often high-grade metamorphism, a relative sparsity of fossils [6], and lack of reliable radiometric dating of tectonic and metamorphic events, are some of the uncertainties in the Piedmont crystalline belts, although recently attempts have been made to learn more about the chronology of metamorphic events, particularly in the southern Piedmont [7-9]. The over- all complex has been subjected to highgrade granu- lite-facies metamorphism with an age of about 440 Ma, based on U/Pb isotopic analyses of zircon frac- tions from the banded gneisses of the Wilmington Complex [15]. Method of analysis Prior to slicing all samples were washed in dilute hydrochloric acid to remove magnetic stains possibly resulting from the field drilling process. In general at least two specimens of 2.5 cm diameter and 2.2 cm length were sliced from each core. One specimen from every third or fourth successive sample was sub- jected to progressive thermal demagnetization from room temperature up to 560°C or 675°C. Remanence measurements were taken in 15-20 steps until the remanence had become too weak for meaningful measurement on our cryogenic magnetometer (below 3 X 10 -3 mA/m) or until excessive build up of a vis- cous remanent magnetization (VRM), apparent after heating at higher temperatures, prevented further remanence measurements. The bulk of the remaining specimens was subjected to partial progressive ther- mal demagnetization in at least 10 steps over a selected temperature interval, generally reaching from 150 to 520°C for the carbonates and up to 560°C for the sandstones. Samples of Devono-Carboniferous to Early Cretaceous age were coUected from 14 localities. Five magnetic components have been distinguished: (1) a predominant compo- nent of recent origin, (2) a secondary component probably acquired during early Tertiary collision of India with Asia or offshore island arcs, (3) primary magnetic components of Middle? Permian to Early Cretaceous age, and another two secondary components either tentatively related with the predominant b-axes pattern of the TSS (4), or attributed to MCT-related metamorphism of the lower TSS (5). Method of analysis Prior to slicing all samples were washed in dilute hydrochloric acid to remove magnetic stains possibly resulting from the field drilling process. In general at least two specimens of 2.5 cm diameter and 2.2 cm length were sliced from each core. This region forms part of India's former leading edge, underthrust by India along the Main Central Thrust (MCT). Samples of Devono-Carboniferous to Early Cretaceous age were coUected from 14 localities. Five magnetic components have been distinguished: (1) a predominant compo- nent of recent origin, (2) a secondary component probably acquired during early Tertiary collision of India with Asia or offshore island arcs, (3) primary magnetic components of Middle? Permian to Early Cretaceous age, and another two secondary components either tentatively related with the predominant b-axes pattern of the TSS (4), or attributed to MCT-related metamorphism of the lower TSS (5). tus in Lower Aptian rocks ([39,40], M. Colchen, personal com- munication, 1980). The lower structural element, the Tibetan Slab, dips monoclinally north. The overlying TSS is unroofed more deeply southwards with lower Palaeo- zoic rocks beautifully exposed in the Nilgiri-Anna- puma massif. Fold axes within the TSS of the Thakkhola graben and of adjacent regions show a minor but consistent westwards plunge [59]. The TSS is characterized structurally by a double vergent setting of folds and thrusts. These are well continu- able along strike, with the thrusts being more pro- nounced to the east of the graben [55]. Four phases of deformation may have occurred between the Middle Eocene and Pleistocene [56]. The earlier three deformation phases are characterized by WNW- ESE-oriented b-axes, with the final phase resulting in large submeridional oriented domes. 4. Samples of Devono-Carboniferous to Early Cretaceous age were coUected from 14 localities. Permian to Early Cretaceous age, and another two secondary components either tentatively related with the predominant b-axes pattern of the TSS (4), or attributed to MCT-related metamorphism of the lower TSS (5). Permian to Early Cretaceous age, and another two secondary components either tentatively related with the predominant b-axes pattern of the TSS (4), or attributed to MCT-related metamorphism of the lower TSS (5). Declinations of the secondary collision component and the primary components mismatch declination data from the Indian subcontinent by 10-15 °. A testable model is proposed, which relates this mismatch to rotational underthrusting of India along the MCT beneath its former leading edge and beneath the Tibetan Plateau. The model accounts for underthrusting of continental lithosphere over 200-350 km at the longitude of the sampled region in central Nepal. A minimum estimate for the northern extent of India (post-Neotethys formation) is proposed, based on this magnitude of rotational underthrusting and on generally accepted values for crustal shortening across the Himalaya. Within the modified Smith and Hallam reconstruction of Gondwanaland, this estimate satisfies constraints imposed by seafloor spreading data from the eastern Indian Ocean and facies analyses of the western Australian continental mar- gin. Declinations of the secondary collision component and the primary components mismatch declination data from the Indian subcontinent by 10-15 °. A testable model is proposed, which relates this mismatch to rotational underthrusting of India along the MCT beneath its former leading edge and beneath the Tibetan Plateau. The model accounts for underthrusting of continental lithosphere over 200-350 km at the longitude of the sampled region in central Nepal. A minimum estimate for the northern extent of India (post-Neotethys formation) is proposed, based on this magnitude of rotational underthrusting and on generally accepted values for crustal shortening across the Himalaya. The overlying TSS is unroofed more deeply southwards with lower Palaeo- zoic rocks beautifully exposed in the Nilgiri-Anna- puma massif. Fold axes within the TSS of the Thakkhola graben and of adjacent regions show a minor but consistent westwards plunge [59]. The TSS is characterized structurally by a double vergent setting of folds and thrusts. These are well continu- able along strike, with the thrusts being more pro- nounced to the east of the graben [55]. Four phases of deformation may have occurred between the Middle Eocene and Pleistocene [56]. The earlier three deformation phases are characterized by WNW- ESE-oriented b-axes, with the final phase resulting in large submeridional oriented domes. 4. The total amount of offset on these faults, however, is only about one third the calculated relative plate motion over the same period. The average rate of dis- placement across the full width of the belt in the last 18,000 years from offset terraces is 16 + 2 mm/yr [5], whereas the plate tectonic rate is 50 mm/yr, similar to the inferred rates from geodetic data for the last 100 years. This discrepancy suggests that only part of the plate motion is taken up by movement on these faults and much of the movement may be occurring as a deformation in the rocks between the faults. If this takes place as a simple shear then reference lines inclined to the direction of shear will be bent. With the rates estimated from geodetic and plate tectonic data the amount of bending could be very substantial; rates of 3 X 10-7/yr simple shear continued for 8 Myr will result in a 67 ° rotation of a line initially per- pendicular to the shear. section_candidates.excerpt: major transcurrent faults striking at about 60-70 ° that offset Late Quaternary river terraces. The total amount of offset on these faults, however, is only about one third the calculated relative plate motion over the same period. The average rate of dis- placement across the full width of the belt in the last 18,000 years from offset terraces is 16 + 2 mm/yr [5], whereas the plate tectonic rate is 50 mm/yr, similar to the inferred rates from geodetic data for the last 100 years. This discrepancy suggests that only part of the plate motion is taken up by movement on these faults and much of the movement may be occurring as a deformation in the rocks between the faults. If this takes place as a simple shear then reference lines inclined to the direction of shear will be bent. With the rates estimated from geodetic and plate tectonic data the amount of bending could be very substantial; rates of 3 X 10-7/yr simple shear continued for 8 Myr will result in a 67 ° rotation of a line initially per- pendicular to the shear. It has been suggested that this bending is caused by relative plate motion in Late Cenozoic times and is continuing today [1 ]. Paleomagnetism The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the specimens was measured either with a spinner magnetometer (PAR) or a "Digico" fluxgate mag- netometer. The following experiments were carried 459 out on two or three specimens for each sample: (1) viscous magnetization evaluation by using the Thellier and Thellier [30] reversal method in the laboratory field, (2) chemical cleaning for about ten days with 6N hydrochloric acid, and (3) step- wise demagnetization comprising about ten steps in an alternating field of up to 38 or 56 mT. Furthermore, the low field susceptibility was measured as a function of the temperature for seven sites uniformly distributed along the dike. The curves were obtained by means of a commer- cial induction bridge (Highmoor) that yields the susceptibility in an alternating field of 1.5 kHz and 0.25 mT. The most magnetic fraction of the rocks separated with an isodynamic Frantz device was used for this measurement. Finally, we determined the anisotropy of susceptibility on two to eight specimens for each site using cores 25 mm in diameter and 22.5 mm long, which had not been demagnetized, but only cleaned with 6N HCI. The susceptibility and anisotropy of susceptibility mea- surements were performed with a commercial a.

The paleomagnetic pole derived from 12 sites regularly distributed along the dike (71°N, 236°E) coincides well with other Mesozoic paleomagnetic poles from the western Africa. A contemporaneous pole from stable Europe is tentatively deduced from African and North American Late Triassic/Early Jurassic poles using different reconstruction models around the North Atlantic Ocean. The divergence between this pole and the Iberian pole corresponds to the result obtained for Permian poles. I. Introduction The Messejana dike of tholeiitic diabase stretches northeasterly over a distance of 530 km, from Odemira on the Atlantic coast in Portugal to Avila in Spain. It is related to the basaltic igneous activity known in the continental zones bordering the central Atlantic Ocean of Late Triassic/Early Jurassic age. The lava flows and intrusive rocks representing the magmatic activity were the sub- ject of many paleomagnetic and geochronologic studies, in western Africa [1,2], Morocco [3,4] and mainly in the eastern Appalachians [5-7]. The authors associate this magmatic activity with the separation of Africa from North America. It marks the initiation of

y known in the continental zones bordering the central Atlantic Ocean of Late Triassic/Early Jurassic age. The lava flows and intrusive rocks representing the magmatic activity were the sub- ject of many paleomagnetic and geochronologic studies, in western Africa [1,2], Morocco [3,4] and mainly in the eastern Appalachians [5-7]. The authors associate this magmatic activity with the separation of Africa from North America. It marks the initiation of rifting or predates it by several tens of millions of years. Occurrences of such Mesozoic diabases are scarce in Europe with the exception of the Iberian Peninsula where the Messejana dike fault system represents a conspicu- ous lineament. No other dolerite dike in the zones around the North Atlantic approaches the di- mension of the Messejana dike except for the Foum Zguid dike in South Morocco. The objectives of the investigation were to pro- vide geochronologic and paleomagnetic informa- tion for a period where the data are rather scarce concerning the Iberian Peninsula as well as Europe. They are useful to elucidate the chronology of the rotation of Iberia relative to Europe and to assess its magnitude. 2. This second volcanic episode was of alkalic nature and rather short-lived compared to the earlier calc- alkalic one. Numerous paleomagnetic studies were carried out on Tertiary volcanics in the last twelv e years, to scrutinize a possible rotation of Sardinia rela- tive to Europe in Oligo-Miocene times. Some con- cluded to a counterclockwise rotation in Oligo- Miocene [1-4], while others challenged this hy- pothesis [5,6]. More recent investigations based on data from about 100 sites, how0cer, favored the counterclockwise rotation [7-9] and ascertained the event at 16-17 Ma age. Reservation had to be made on this conclusion since the samplings for K-Ar dating and paleomagnetic investigations had been performed independently. Serious doubts arose whether both informations pertained to the same object or not. Furthermore, the ignimbritic series was almost ignored in those correlations. The aim of the present work is two-fold: (1) to discuss the numerous available paleomagnetic data from a statistical point of view in order to assess the amplitude of the rotation; (2) to determine the time of the rotation by K

As the secular variation causes a great inclination change near the equator, the steep positive inclination of IS 123 278 may be explained by the geomagnetic secular change. Steep inclination values of the Miocene Bilungala Volcanics also may be due to the secular variation and/or due to the tectonic tilting accom- panied by Miocene uplift in the northern part of Sulawesi [6]. One of the difficulties in working with rocks near the equator is that the inclination data are usually a reliable index of polarity. However, the polarity can be determined from the declination change as a function of time. It is noted that there are no specimens whose remanent magnetizations are either in a northwest or southeast direction (Fig. 3). section_candidates.excerpt: closely comparable with successions in the Banda Arc islands of Timor and Ceram and with parts of Australia. In the Western Province which consists of the southern and northern arms, a pre-Cretaceous metamorphic basement is over- lain by volcanic and clastic successions of Tertiary and Quaternary age and associated plutonic intru- sions. Several hypotheses have been put forth to ex- plain the origin of the K-shaped morphology of Sulawesi from a geological viewpoint [6-10]. A paleomagnetic study offers an independent method for testing these hypotheses. During the course of an expedition to the northern arm of Sulawesi in 1978, samples were taken from the Gorontalo and Menado regions for paleomagnetic study. In this paper, we examine the hypothesis of a clockwise rotation of the northern arm of Sulawesi using the results obtained from a paleomagnetic study. 2. Geology and sampling In the Gorontalo area (see Fig. 1), the basement consists of Eocene to early Miocene oceanic basalt and minor pelagic sediments of the Tinombo For- mation [11]. These basement rocks are overlaid with intermediate and acid calc-alkaline volcanics of Miocene age (Bilungala Volcanics). Several hypotheses have been put forth to ex- plain the origin of the K-shaped morphology of Sulawesi from a geological viewpoint [6-10]. A paleomagnetic study offers an independent method for testing these hypotheses. During the course of an expedition to the northern arm of Sulawesi in 1978, samples were taken from the Gorontalo and Menado regions for paleomagnetic study. In the Western Province which consists of the southern and northern arms, a pre-Cretaceous metamorphic basement is over- lain by volcanic and clastic successions of Tertiary and Quaternary age and associated plutonic intru- sions. Several hypotheses have been put forth to ex- plain the origin of the K-shaped morphology of Sulawesi from a geological viewpoint [6-10]. A paleomagnetic study offers an independent method for testing these hypotheses. During the course of an expedition to the northern arm of Sulawesi in 1978, samples were taken from the Gorontalo and Menado regions for paleomagnetic study. In this paper, we examine the hypothesis of a clockwise rotation of the northern arm of Sulawesi using the results obtained from a paleomagnetic study. 2. The study employs the principle that higher structural levels passed through their blocking temperatures earlier than lower levels and therefore record earlier pole positions, and it utilises dolerites and diorites intruded late in, or after, the tectonic history to minimise anisotropy effects. In the amphibolite facies terrain at Qaqatoqaq (1400 m) highly-stable magnetite-held remanences move on demagnetlsation progressively along small circles interpreted to record younger to older apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) motions during cooling through the blocking temperature ranges. Directions of magnetization No conclusive evidence, such as conglomerate or fold tests, yet exists to demonstrate an early age for the magnetization. Therefore, paleomagnetic directions reported here are considered pre- liminary. Although petrographic observations sug- gest that much of the hematite pigment is pre- diagenetic, they shed no light as to the amount of time required for hematite formation. Studies are planned to provide information on the time of acquisition of the magnetization. Directions of magnetization after partial ther- mal demagnetization are plotted in Fig. 5 for sam- pies from each site. The mean NRM and cleaned directions for each site are also plotted in Fig. 5 and are listed in Table 1. Westerly declinations, with corresponding pole positions in the Pacific Ocean, are considered to be normal polarity, fol- lowing the convention employed for directi

tratigraphic distributions and the negative inclinations of both polarities suggest the presence of a stable, negative- inclination, secondary component of magnetiza- tion. This inference is supported by eight samples, not shown on Fig. 5, which have directions be- tween those of the normal and reversed endpoints. Because directions from the eight samples, which probably contain nearly equal amounts of both components of magnetization, did not shift signifi- cantly during demagnetization, blocking tempera- ture spectra are probably similar for both compo- nents of magnetization. Secondary specular hema- tite was seen in polished thin sections, which prob- ably is the principal source of this stable sec- ondary magnetization. An approximate primary direction of magnetization can be obtained by averaging the normal direction and the anti-pole of the reversed-polarity mean direction. Although statistics cannot be obtained from such an aver- age, the resulting direction probably is more nearly correct than either the normal- or reversed-polarity mean direction. The C-I group magnetization is a stable direction (D=332 °, I= + 18 °) with unblocking temperatures (Tun) between 550 and 650°C, present in the older Covey Hill Formation; this direction is probably a chemical remanence acquired during the Covey Hill diagenesis and carried predominantly by hematite. The main reason for the scarcity of palaeomagnetic information for the Late Jurassic/Early Cretaceous is that very weakly magnetized rocks were formed during this period. The development of extremely sensitive magne- tometers now permits the investigation of these rocks but the accumulation of data has been slow. One reason for this is that the demagnetization response of the samples is often more positive to the time-consuming thermal treatment than to the faster AF technique. The purpose of this paper is to establish a land-based reversal stratigraphy for a poorly known part of the Mesozoic polarity time scale, e.g. Upper Kimmeridgian/Berriasian. 2. As a group, the paleomagnetic declination values of the samples systematically decrease with age. This decrease is attributed to progressive anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu during the process of formation of the North Fiji Basin. A linear least squares analysis of the paleomagnetic data indicates that the island has rotated in an anticlockwise direction through 90 ° during the past 7 m.y. at a rate of 13.7 ° per million years. Declination values as low as 245 ° measured for some sites (not dated) suggest that anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu and development of the North Fiji Basin could have commenced as early as 10 m.y. B.P. following the breakup of the ancient Solomons-New Hebrides-Fiji-Lau island arc. Large rotations of microplates may have occurred along other island arcs and marginal basin systems elsewhere in the Western Pacific and such rotational histories may reflect in detail the evolutionary development of these arcs and basins. 1. Introduction Rotational tectonic features such as the spiral system of islands in the Banda Sea Arc of In- donesia and the curved Fiji-Lau Ridge island arc system (Fig.

onic features such as the spiral system of islands in the Banda Sea Arc of In- donesia and the curved Fiji-Lau Ridge island arc system (Fig. 1) are readily apparent from observa- tions of bathymetric maps. Based on a study of the regional bathymetric maps of the North Fiji Basin [1], Malahoff [2] proposed that the Fijian Islands had undergone anticlockwise rotation (Fig. 2). Further evidence for such a rotation is presented in this paper in the form of initial paleomagnetic and radiometric age results which together show that there has been a progressive rotation of the horizontal paleomagnetic vector (declination) through time. Paleomagnetic results from 15 volcanic sites indicate an anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu through about 90 ° during the past 7 m.y. In another recent study, Malahoff et al. [3] conducted a detailed aeromagnetic survey of the North Fiji Basin. ic analysis of the dated rocks shows declination vectors ranging from 325 + 9 ° for an age of 2.9--+0.2 m.y.B.P, to 290-+4 ° for an age of 7.0-+0.4 m.y.B.P. As a group, the paleomagnetic declination values of the samples systematically decrease with age. This decrease is attributed to progressive anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu during the process of formation of the North Fiji Basin. A linear least squares analysis of the paleomagnetic data indicates that the island has rotated in an anticlockwise direction through 90 ° during the past 7 m.y. at a rate of 13.7 ° per million years. Declination values as low as 245 ° measured for some sites (not dated) suggest that anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu and development of the North Fiji Basin could have commenced as early as 10 m.y. B.P. following the breakup of the ancient Solomons-New Hebrides-Fiji-Lau island arc. Large rotations of microplates may have occurred along other island arcs and marginal basin systems elsewhere in the Western Pacific and such rotational histories may reflect in detail the evolutionary development of these arcs and basins. 1. Introduction Rotational tectonic features such as the spiral system of islands in the Banda Sea Arc of In- donesia and the curved Fiji-Lau Ridge island arc system (Fig.

onic features such as the spiral system of islands in the Banda Sea Arc of In- donesia and the curved Fiji-Lau Ridge island arc system (Fig. 1) are readily apparent from observa- tions of bathymetric maps. Based on a study of the regional bathymetric maps of the North Fiji Basin [1], Malahoff [2] proposed that the Fijian Islands had undergone anticlockwise rotation (Fig. 2). Further evidence for such a rotation is presented in this paper in the form of initial paleomagnetic and radiometric age results which together show that there has been a progressive rotation of the horizontal paleomagnetic vector (declination) through time. Paleomagnetic results from 15 volcanic sites indicate an anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu through about 90 ° during the past 7 m.y. In another recent study, Malahoff et al. [3] conducted a detailed aeromagnetic survey of the North Fiji Basin. Results from this study suggest the presence of magnetic anomalies 1 to 4 (0-7.8 m.y.B.P.) within the North Fiji Basin and the location of a currently active spreading center to the west of the Fijian Islands. Volcanic centers elsewhere, such as those located along the Hawaiian Ridge [11] and the New Hebrides island arc [2], form along distinct crustal rifts, which are, in turn, formed along predominant directions of litho- spheric stress. Linear magnetic anomalies associ- ated with such volcanic centers are usually located above dike swarms comprised of highly mag- netized rocks [2,11]. Similarly, the Tavua volcanic center is marked by the presence of high-amplitude 401 total magnetic force anomalies of up to 1500 nT peak to peak (Fig. 4), and marks the site of rocks with unusually high intensities of magnetization. The magnetic anomaly map shown in Fig. 4 was constructed from Project Magnet flights [12] car- ried out over the island of Viti Levu at an altitude of 2200 m. The source of the high-amplitude mag- netic anomaly located over the Tavua volcanic center is interpreted to be a highly magnetized volcanic plug with associated dikes, or dike swarms, that may have been intruded as a result of regional tectonic stresses generated during the development of the island. The analyses shown in Fig. 5 suggest that the source bodies for the magnetic anomalies associated with the Tavua volcano radiate away from the Tavua volcanic center. Intensities of natural remanent magnetiza- tion (Fig. 6) of rock samples taken from the ex- posures of rocks from the Mba volcanic group in the vicinity of the Tavua volcanic center agree well with the areal distribution of the total magnetic force anomalies shown in Fig. 5. The Mba Volcanic group is a mapping unit of the geological map of Viti Levu [9] and consists of rocks that are largely Neogene andesites and basalts. Volcanic centers elsewhere, such as those located along the Hawaiian Ridge [11] and the New Hebrides island arc [2], form along distinct crustal rifts, which are, in turn, formed along predominant directions of litho- spheric stress. Linear magnetic anomalies associ- ated with such volcanic centers are usually located above dike swarms comprised of highly mag- netized rocks [2,11]. Similarly, the Tavua volcanic center is marked by the presence of high-amplitude 401 total magnetic force anomalies of up to 1500 nT peak to peak (Fig. 4), and marks the site of rocks with unusually high intensities of magnetization. The magnetic anomaly map shown in Fig. 4 was constructed from Project Magnet flights [12] car- ried out over the island of Viti Levu at an altitude of 2200 m. The source of the high-amplitude mag- netic anomaly located over the Tavua volcanic center is interpreted to be a highly magnetized volcanic plug with associated dikes, or dike swarms, that may have been intruded as a result of regional tectonic stresses generated during the development of the island. As a group, the paleomagnetic declination values of the samples systematically decrease with age. This decrease is attributed to progressive anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu during the process of formation of the North Fiji Basin. A linear least squares analysis of the paleomagnetic data indicates that the island has rotated in an anticlockwise direction through 90 ° during the past 7 m.y. at a rate of 13.7 ° per million years. Declination values as low as 245 ° measured for some sites (not dated) suggest that anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu and development of the North Fiji Basin could have commenced as early as 10 m.y. B.P. following the breakup of the ancient Solomons-New Hebrides-Fiji-Lau island arc. Large rotations of microplates may have occurred along other island arcs and marginal basin systems elsewhere in the Western Pacific and such rotational histories may reflect in detail the evolutionary development of these arcs and basins. 1. Introduction Rotational tectonic features such as the spiral system of islands in the Banda Sea Arc of In- donesia and the curved Fiji-Lau Ridge island arc system (Fig.

onic features such as the spiral system of islands in the Banda Sea Arc of In- donesia and the curved Fiji-Lau Ridge island arc system (Fig. 1) are readily apparent from observa- tions of bathymetric maps. Based on a study of the regional bathymetric maps of the North Fiji Basin [1], Malahoff [2] proposed that the Fijian Islands had undergone anticlockwise rotation (Fig. 2). Further evidence for such a rotation is presented in this paper in the form of initial paleomagnetic and radiometric age results which together show that there has been a progressive rotation of the horizontal paleomagnetic vector (declination) through time. Paleomagnetic results from 15 volcanic sites indicate an anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu through about 90 ° during the past 7 m.y. In another recent study, Malahoff et al. [3] conducted a detailed aeromagnetic survey of the North Fiji Basin. Thus the highly dispersed direc- tions from this site were not surprising. Site 9 had anomalous rock magnetic properties. The rema- nence was found to reside in a carrier of high coercivity (greater than 100 mT) which, by com- parison with the low coercivities found in the other sites suggests that alteration of the magnetic mineralogy has taken place. The field appearance of this site is also different from the other sites. The samples have a tan color in contrast to the gray and bluish gray samples from the other sites. The high coercivities, poor paleomagnetic reliabil- ity, and the tan color of the samples from site 9 suggest that it has been exposed to recent oxida- tion which has destroyed its paleomagnetic proper- ties. Site 4 was similar both in lithology and rock magnetic characteristics to the other good sites and we are unable to explain its poor paleomagnetic reliability. The sampling area in northwest Wyoming lies in the area where the overthrust belt impinges upon basement uplifts on the foreland (Fig. 1). Samles were taken where limestone outcrops were accessible, and where the beds were tilted so that a fold test could be applied [12]. The sites are in the Prospect Thrust (sites l-5), the Darby Thrust (sites 9-13), and from the Gros Ventre Block (sites 6-8) which is a basement uplift on the foreland. Since rotations have been documented in Triassic strata in the overthrust belt [ 131, the sites on the foreland are particularly important. They serve as a control to test for bias in the mean direction due to the rotation of thrust sheets.
